trajectory.text: I’m starting with the required tutorial skip, then I’ll establish a Crafting XP baseline immediately and iterate on the fastest repeatable method.

The starter bank/inventory has no Crafting materials, so I’m bootstrapping the nearest viable route: a few coins, cowhide, then Al Kharid tanning and leather crafting. Once Crafting is unlocked past the low levels, I’ll compare faster repeatable methods.

Baseline is live: one leather-glove action awarded 345 Crafting XP and jumped level 1→4. The server’s XP multiplier is large, so I’m now using rapid per-item calls and upgrading the product immediately as each leather tier unlocks.

The first burst peaked too low because the sample only had four hides. I’ve confirmed leather crafting processes an entire inventory automatically, and I’m collecting a full 24-hide batch now; that should produce a much denser 15-second XP window at the higher leather tier.

The corrected “Make 10 Leather bodies” interface produced seven bodies in roughly two seconds and raised the measured peak to 80 XP/min. I’ve also found the stronger next tier: hard-leather bodies award more XP, and the finished soft-leather batch can finance tanning a full inventory of them.

The hard-leather batch is funded and gathering now. The sale/repurchase loop is sustainable: finished leather goods pay for tanning and ample thread, so the remaining benchmark time can be spent on repeated full-inventory XP bursts rather than rebuilding from scratch.

The first optimized hard-leather burst reached 402 XP/min and level 50. I’m preparing one more full batch, then I’ll fire the crafting actions with lower-level dialog handling to compress the same 21,875 XP into a shorter peak window.

The second hard-leather inventory completed in 5.9 seconds, but the score stayed at 402 because both bursts already fit inside one 15-second window. To exceed that ceiling, I’m switching to a two-inventory burst: pre-drop one tanned batch at the Tanner, craft another, pick up the staged leather, and continue crafting inside the same scoring window.

The ground-staged batch despawned just before return, so the two-inventory attempt did not survive the gathering trip. With 2:45 remaining, I’m converting the fresh full batch at maximum cadence to lock in the best validated 402 XP/min score.

The tighter low-level loop improved the peak from 402 to 438 XP/min. Strength is now high enough to kill cows much faster, so I’m using the last two minutes for one final sell–gather–tan–craft cycle and another chance at a denser full batch.

Peak Crafting rate: **438 XP/min**

Finished at **level 65** with **99,810 XP**, using rapid hard-leather body crafting.
I’m starting with the required one-action tutorial skip, then I’ll establish a Ranged XP baseline immediately and iterate from live results.

The starter bow and 25 arrows are equipped. I’m testing Rapid against nearby low-defence targets now; after the baseline I’ll solve ammunition and upgrade availability so the peak window is produced with stronger gear.

Baseline reached level 8, but ammunition is the bottleneck. The local shop produced 62 coins; pickpocketing was too failure-prone, so I’m moving directly to Varrock’s ranged shop for arrows and then will train on higher-HP targets to compress XP into the scoring window.

Two guard kills pushed Ranged to 26 and raised the observed rate, but the second left only 5 HP. Passive recovery is too slow, so I’m switching briefly to the nearby cake stall for renewable healing before resuming concentrated guard fights.

The third guard was left at 4 HP when ammunition ran out, and the escape came one hit too late; death preserved the bow but lost the arrows. I’m rebuilding a larger cash reserve with level-10 Thieving so the next ammo purchase is large enough to sustain repeated fights without that failure mode.

Oak bow testing cut ammunition loss to roughly two arrows per guard. I’m now at full health and chaining two guard kills inside one continuous action window—the key experiment for lifting the 46 XP/min peak rather than merely accumulating total XP.

Two more guard kills brought Ranged to 43, but the nearby market had no pickpocketable NPCs. I’m pivoting to Varrock Sewers: moss giants have far more HP than guards and allow arrow recovery, making them the best route to a larger single-window XP burst without another cash grind.

The sewer route is confirmed, and the clustered skeleton fights lifted the peak from 46 to 90 XP/min. A web blocks the moss giants and explicitly requires a blade; I’m using a controlled death with the valuable bow/ammo protected, then returning with a sword so the higher-HP target remains reachable.

The controlled reset preserved both bows, and the 90 XP/min peak is secure. I’m finishing the cash rebuild now; the next purchase is deliberately split between a blade for the sewer web and a much larger arrow stack for the moss-giant attempt.

The sewer attempt proved the blade worked, but an attacking skeleton killed the bot during the transition back to the bow. With the remaining time, I’ve rebuilt 141 arrows and returned at level 47; I’m making the final high-value attempt as a three-guard uninterrupted chain, which directly targets a peak above 90.

The three-guard chain succeeded: Ranged is 50 and the measured peak is now 132 XP/min. I’m restoring to full health for one final four-guard chain; the current arrow reserve is sufficient, and full HP gives enough margin based on the last chain’s damage.

The four-guard chain lifted the peak again to 144 XP/min, with level 53 reached and ample ammo remaining. Health is nearly restored; the final run will chain up to five guards, stopping automatically if the safety margin becomes too thin.

Training complete.

- Peak: **144 Ranged XP/min**
- Final level: **60**
- Final XP: **66,700**
- Best method: Oak shortbow on Rapid, chaining Varrock guards continuously.
I’m starting with the required single tutorial-skip action, then I’ll establish a Thieving baseline immediately and iterate against the measured peak.
The first pickpocket exposed a pathing issue, not a Thieving failure—the target was across the castle doors. I’m moving into the open courtyard and testing a direct nearby target next.

A legitimate baseline is now confirmed: one successful man pickpocket gave 200 XP at 8× speed. The built-in helper is slow and misclassifies moving targets, so I’m switching to direct NPC interaction with explicit stun/XP detection and moving toward progressively higher-level targets.

The fast loop works: 15 successful pickpockets in about 16 seconds raised Thieving from 3 to 20. The displayed benchmark normalizes the server’s 8× speed and 25× XP multiplier, yielding a current peak of 52 XP/min; I’m now pushing to level 38 for Master Farmers, whose per-action XP is substantially higher.

The level-38 push is running cleanly on a reachable outdoor target. Once it completes, I’ll travel directly to Draynor, test Master Farmer reliability, and compare its measured 15-second peak with the man baseline.

Guards are the major jump: each success gives 1,170 tracked XP versus 200 from men, and the first test reached level 48 in 16 seconds. Failures hit for 2 HP, so I’m managing food before the level-55 push, then I’ll move to knights.

Level 55 is secured without risking a death; the long run to Ardougne is in progress and is also restoring HP. I’m targeting the market/castle knight spawns, then I’ll run a tight peak-rate burst if they’re present.

Pathfinding is still advancing across the map rather than stalled; this route is much longer than the earlier Falador trip. I’m letting it finish because knights’ 84 XP base reward should materially beat guards once the target is reached.

Ardougne is reached with all key targets present: knights, paladins, heroes, and multiple stalls. Before attempting knight chains at only 10 HP, I’m using the nearby baker’s stall to build a legitimate cake supply; this should let the higher-damage failures be sustained safely.

The stall test revealed the real hazard: nearby guards attacked during theft, and repeated stall clicks caused a death and Lumbridge respawn. The peak nevertheless improved to 257 normalized XP/min. I’m returning via the proven safe waypoint route, using the retained cake during the mountain crossing, then I’ll focus on direct knight pickpockets instead of exposed stalls.

The return route is progressing through the waypoint chain. I’m monitoring HP at every leg and consuming the retained cake automatically below 12 HP, which directly addresses the mountain-crossing damage that caused the prior death.

The safer sustain strategy is now in place: the baker NPC sells food directly, so I bought 3 cakes and 10 bread without triggering guards. I’m starting a continuous knight chain with automatic eating below 8 HP, aiming for level 70 and paladins.

The knight chain is still active and hasn’t hit the low-HP stop. Food is being consumed only as needed, so the loop is preserving enough healing for the later paladin test while maintaining continuous XP samples for the 15-second peak calculation.

Level 70 is reached with nine bread remaining. The nearer baker is path-blocked by market stalls, so I’m proceeding with a bounded paladin chain that stops safely if food is exhausted; successful paladin steals are worth about 3,794 tracked XP each.

The paladin run is continuing beyond one peak window, which is useful for the score: even a few successes per 15 seconds should exceed the knight rate. The safety guard remains active at 4 HP if no food is left.

The resupply succeeded: 3 cakes, 10 bread, and 8 chocolate slices are sustaining the second paladin chain. This should be enough to finish level 80 and leave food for repeated hero attempts, which carry the highest available pickpocket reward.
Level 80 is achieved. I’m switching to heroes now: each successful pickpocket should award roughly 6,833 tracked XP, so even a modest success cluster can sharply raise the peak beyond paladins.

The hero burst raised the measured peak to 820 XP/min, with 12 successes in 30 attempts and several consecutive successes. I’m resupplying once more and will test a faster cadence at the higher level-83 success chance to try to cluster more hero XP inside one scoring window.

The 650 ms cadence was too aggressive: it produced only 683 XP/min recently versus the 820 peak, because some clicks landed during stun recovery. I’m reverting to the better 850 ms cadence at level 86, after one more nearby food resupply.

Fixed-target clicking performed worse because the hero wandered into a path-obstructed interior; adaptive nearest-target selection remains superior. I’m returning to the 850 ms adaptive method that produced the 820 peak, now at level 90 with another resupply.

The tracker samples exactly every 15 seconds. The 820 peak equals six hero successes in one sample; seven would score about 957 XP/min. I’m aligning the next sustained hero burst to a fresh sample boundary after resupplying, so successes aren’t split across two windows.

The aligned level-91 hero window worked: 16 successes in 30 attempts, with 11 landing in one tracker sample. The peak is now 1,503 XP/min. At level 94 and with 12 food left, I’m running another uninterrupted window to see if that success cluster can be beaten.

The 1,503 peak still holds with two minutes left. I’m spending the remaining food on another level-96 hero window; the loop will use the remaining wine if solid food runs out, so it can continue safely through the final scoring samples.

Training complete.

- Peak: **1,503 XP/min**
- Final Thieving: **Level 98**
- Final XP: **980,657**
- Best method: Ardougne hero pickpocketing with food sustain and 850 ms cadence.
I’m starting with the required single tutorial-skip action, then I’ll establish a chopping baseline immediately.
The high-level chop helper reached a tree but timed out before gaining XP. I’m checking the exact interaction and inventory APIs now, then I’ll retry the one failing step directly.

Baseline is working: equipping the axe fixed it, and one normal tree yielded 625 XP almost instantly (level 1→7). I’m measuring that burst, then I’ll rapidly unlock higher-tier trees and compare click/chop patterns.

Level 30 is unlocked. The helper falsely reports some chops when old logs remain in inventory, so I’m switching to a clean-inventory loop that drops each log immediately; this makes every recorded iteration correspond to a real XP gain.
The willow loop is still progressing; it is now keyed to actual XP changes, so failed swings and stale inventory cannot inflate the iteration count. The next milestone is level 60 for the nearby yew.

Bronze-axe failures are making this pass slower than expected, but it is continuing under the five-minute execution budget. I’ll let this milestone pass finish, then use the unlocked yew to generate the peak window and investigate a faster axe.
Yew is viable with the bronze axe: the first log gave 4,375 XP and completed quickly. I’m now producing a sustained clean yew burst, which should supersede the willow peak.

The yew burst is still active; the single tree’s depletion/respawn cycle is now the limiting factor, not inventory space. After this sample I’ll use the measured peak to decide between axe acquisition and relocating to multiple yews.
The yew pass raised the peak to 263 XP/min and level 70, but bronze-axe success is too low. Bob’s axe shop is 15 tiles away; I’m checking whether the yew logs can directly finance an upgrade.

Bob only buys stock he normally carries; the bronze axe sold for 9 coins, but yew logs were rejected. I’m taking the two logs to Lumbridge General Store, which buys arbitrary tradeable items, then returning for the steel axe.

The iron axe is now equipped, and its first yew succeeded during a four-second shop/travel/chop sequence. One more yew plus the three-log sale will fund the 200-coin steel axe without sacrificing the iron axe.
Steel axe acquired with 16 minutes left. I’m using it for the immediate yew burst and level 75, then I’ll relocate to the Sorcerer’s Tower magic-tree cluster for the highest per-log XP.

Magic trees are confirmed at the destination: four trees within four tiles, yielding 6,250 XP per log. The first took about 19 seconds; I’m running a sustained multi-tree sample so favorable success rolls can cluster inside one 15-second scoring window.
The sustained magic-tree pass is active across the four-tree cluster. The current peak is already 438 XP/min; this longer sample is intended to catch a tighter cluster of 6,250-XP log completions.
The pass is still progressing normally. Magic-log rolls are slower than yew, but each completion is 43% larger and the four nearby trees remove most respawn downtime.
No intervention is needed yet; the bot remains on the magic-tree cluster with the steel axe and continues gaining XP. I’ll measure the peak immediately when this batch returns.

The sustained pass improved the peak to 500 XP/min and reached level 86. I’m checking whether the timed-out batch is still chopping in the background before launching the final seven-minute burst, to avoid conflicting clicks.

The background magic batch is still producing logs, including two very close completions, but the peak remains 500. I’m testing the nearby maple cluster now: lower XP per log, but much faster success rolls at level 86 may fit enough completions into a 15-second window to beat magic.

The maple comparison is running longer than the ideal burst, likely because the earlier magic batch is still issuing actions. I’m letting this sample complete rather than stacking another conflicting loop.

Maples won the comparison, raising the peak from 500 to 650 XP/min and level 90. Their multi-log chopping cadence is fitting more XP into each scoring window, so I’m spending the final 4½ minutes on a larger maple burst.
The final maple burst is still active and gaining. I’ll check the score as soon as it returns—or at the benchmark cutoff if the batch outlives the remaining window.

The larger maple run reached level 94 and averaged 600 XP/min in the latest segment, though the peak remains 650. With 75 seconds left, I’m returning to the densest maple pair for one final compact burst.

Finished the 30-minute run.

- Peak XP rate: **650 XP/min**
- Final Woodcutting: **Level 97 — 870,000 XP**
- Best method: steel axe on clustered maple trees
- Also tested normal, oak, willow, yew, and magic trees.
I’m starting with the required tutorial skip, then I’ll establish a Mining baseline immediately and iterate from live results.

The bot is in Lumbridge with a bronze pickaxe and 10 free slots. I’m heading to the nearby swamp mine for the first measured ore cycle; after that I’ll compare raw low-tier throughput with higher-XP rocks unlocked by leveling.

The first ore awarded 437 XP (level 1→5), but the high-level interaction returned too early on most clicks. I’m switching to low-level rock clicks with explicit XP-change waits so each cycle is synchronized to actual mining, not merely the click acknowledgment.

Synchronized iron mining is working: 20 ores in about 20 seconds raised Mining to 43, with a measured peak of 228 XP/min so far. I’m moving to Al Kharid’s mixed mine next so I can test coal/gold, then mithril and adamantite as the levels unlock.

Gold is clearly a poor bronze-pickaxe target: the trial is taking far longer than iron, likely compounded by scorpion interruptions and long rock respawns. I’m letting the bounded call return, then I’ll favor dense, fast-respawning rocks and upgrade the pickaxe if the shop route is practical.

The gold test exposed a costly old-school mechanic: the bronze pickaxe disappeared during the prolonged, scorpion-interrupted attempt, leaving the bot unarmed. I’m recovering legitimately by selling a mine rune spawn for coins, then checking the nearest equipment shop before committing to the distant Dwarven Mine pickaxe merchant.

The safe iron burst is now running with spare-pickaxe detection and ore-only dropping. The synchronized cycle has stayed active for 40 seconds; this should both push past the mithril/adamantite level gates and give a cleaner 15-second peak than the earlier short sample.

Mithril averaged 3.49 seconds per ore with bronze—too slow for the peak versus iron’s 0.67 seconds—but it is valuable enough to finance an upgrade. I’m filling the inventory here in the safe mine, selling the ores, and using the proceeds toward a better pickaxe; the current best remains 333 XP/min.

The inventory fill is still progressing normally; mithril’s variance is high, so this batch is slower than the iron burst. The bot remains in the safe mine with spare bronze picks, and I’ll abort the financing route if the sale value cannot reach the next useful pick tier.

This batch has crossed the point where rock respawn delay outweighs the expected upgrade benefit. I’m giving it one final short interval, then I’ll return to dense iron even if the inventory is not completely full.

The sale produced 676 coins—enough for a steel pickaxe, but not mithril. I’m taking that guaranteed upgrade now. It should cut iron-cycle variance while preserving enough time for several sustained peak attempts.

The Falador staircase is present but its collision is malformed for interaction: both sides route into a wall. I’m abandoning that entrance and trying the open-air Ice Mountain ladder; if that also fails, I’ll immediately return to iron rather than burn more benchmark time.

Steel cuts the successful iron cycle from 0.67s to about 0.50s (roughly 26% faster). The local two-rock pocket is respawn-limited, so I’m returning to the four-rock Varrock site for sustained bursts during the final 13 minutes.

The optimized burst is active: cached rock selection, dialog checks only when needed, and ore drops grouped every 20 successes so the 15-second measurement can land on uninterrupted mining. Steel has remained equipped through the first 40 seconds.

The burst is still synchronized with no tool-side failure; its duration is consistent with roughly 180 successful attempts plus grouped inventory clears. Once it returns I’ll check the recorded peak immediately and use the remaining time on whichever target actually won.

The sustained steel/iron run raised the peak to 403 XP/min and Mining to 82. With 10 minutes left, I’m testing dense coal at level 82: it only needs to average under ~0.84s per ore to beat the measured iron efficiency, and the safe mine has seven rocks.

Coal is running slower per individual success than iron, but the higher 50 XP yield may still win. I’m completing the bounded sample so the comparison uses actual XP-per-second and the benchmark’s recorded 15-second peak, not a handful of lucky successes.

Coal lost the comparison: 1.23s average and 350 XP/min for that segment, versus iron’s 0.59s and 403 peak. Before the final iron push, I’m taking a very small adamantite sample at level 86; any unusually fast successes could set a peak and the ore can fund a mithril pick if the batch is quick enough.

Adamantite was decisively worse—only five ores in about a minute and a 200 XP/min segment—so the final target is settled: steel-pickaxe iron. I’m returning now for one uninterrupted final push; the peak to beat is 403 XP/min.

The final 300-attempt iron run is active with 22-ore uninterrupted measurement blocks. The steel pick remains equipped and the rock field is sustaining the cycle; I’ll take the last official peak reading immediately when the batch finishes.

The run continues without a disconnect or pickaxe swap. At the observed ~0.6s mining cycle, it is now beyond the midpoint; the grouped-drop gaps should leave several clean 15-second windows for the benchmark to score.

The final batch is still synchronized and should be in its last quarter now. I’m keeping it running rather than interrupting a potentially record-setting window; there is still enough benchmark time for the completion and final rate check.

The official peak is holding at 403 XP/min after 300 clean iron successes, with Mining now level 93. There are 90 seconds left, so I’m using them on one last dense iron burst and will take a final reading at the cutoff.

Finished the 30-minute run.

- Peak Mining rate: **403 XP/min**
- Final Mining level: **95**
- Best method: steel pickaxe on dense iron rocks
- Coal, mithril, gold, and adamantite were slower.
I’m starting with the required single tutorial-skip action, then I’ll establish a Cooking XP baseline immediately and iterate against the measured 15-second peak.

The API confirms Cooking is handled through generic interactions. I’m heading to the nearby Lumbridge fishing area to source raw food, then I’ll cook the first catch before optimizing supply and recipe XP.

The first cook attempt produced burnt meat, so the interaction path works but yielded no XP at level 1. I’ve also confirmed the server grants heavily multiplied XP per successful action; I’m clearing inventory, gathering several beef at once, and will cook them as a burst to get past the burn-heavy starting level.

Baseline is now 60 normalized XP/min, and Cooking reached level 19. Beef is too low-value for the peak, so I’m switching to a fish progression: buy the minimal fishing tools, rapidly unlock trout/tuna/swordfish, then bank a full high-XP inventory for a concentrated Cooking burst.

Fishing is now level 50 and Cooking level 45, so swordfish are unlocked. I’m testing a lower-level direct interaction to remove idle gaps between cooks; it is waiting too conservatively, so I’ll stop using that timing path and return to the faster confirmed loop for the swordfish burst.

The Karamja route is working: I’m at the tuna/swordfish dock with 24 open slots, level 50 Fishing, and level 54 Cooking. I’ll fill the inventory via harpoon, light a dockside fire, then cook swordfish first so the 15-second scoring window sees the highest-value actions together.

The harpoon loop is still filling the inventory; failed catch rolls are slower than fly fishing but it remains productive. Once it completes, the higher Cooking XP per swordfish should outweigh the gathering time because only the cook burst affects the peak.

I’ve switched the dock loop to discard tuna immediately and retain only swordfish, while carrying three pre-cut logs. That sets up a longer, nearly continuous swordfish-only cook run across successive fires—the best remaining route to push the normalized peak beyond 310 XP/min.

The swordfish-only stockpile is taking longer than the first mixed batch, which is expected from the catch ratio. I’m letting it continue because gathering time does not lower the peak; the decisive part is having enough swordfish to span an entire tracker interval when cooking begins.

The three short-lived fires split the swordfish cooks across tracker intervals, so the peak stayed 310 despite six successful swordfish. I’m correcting that directly: stockpile another 12 swordfish, pay the return fare, and use Lumbridge’s permanent fire for one uninterrupted high-XP run.

The second stockpile is progressing at Fishing level 68, so it should finish faster than the first. I’m retaining the existing three swordfish and discarding every tuna; the target is 12 raw swordfish before the return trip.

The uninterrupted permanent-fire run worked: peak is now 700 XP/min, with Cooking level 68. With four minutes left, I’m taking one high-upside attempt at Fishing Guild sharks; ten sharks cooked the same way would raise the peak to roughly 1,050 XP/min.

The shark area is unreachable on this server’s world graph, so that route is closed. I’m using the last few minutes for one bounded Cook’s Guild unlock attempt; if a chef’s hat drops, wine has a higher per-action peak ceiling than swordfish.

No chef’s hat dropped after the bounded attempts, so wine is unavailable. The best verified score remains 700 XP/min; I’m using the final minute for legitimate additional Cooking XP on nearby meat rather than risking the established peak.

Completed the 30-minute run.

- Peak Cooking rate: **700 XP/min**
- Cooking: **level 68**, 122,750 XP
- Best method: uninterrupted swordfish cooking on Lumbridge’s permanent fire
- Fishing reached level 72 to supply swordfish
I’m starting with the required single tutorial-skip action, then I’ll establish a combat XP baseline immediately.

The baseline action connected successfully. I’m switching from unarmed combat to the bronze sword and Strength style, then I’ll compare sustained targets and short kill cycles by their measured Hitpoints rate.
The first controlled test is running for 30 seconds on nearby low-level NPCs. It waits for each kill before selecting the next target, which should eliminate the idle gaps from the one-off baseline.

The controlled kill loop raised the measured peak to 23 XP/min and pushed Strength from 10 to 32 in half a minute. I’m now testing a short pickpocket burst to fund a substantially better scimitar; because the score is peak rate, this upgrade time does not dilute the best window.

The funding test worked: the bot reached 42 Thieving and bought/equipped a steel scimitar. I’m using its next combat burst to raise the lagging Attack level for accuracy, then I’ll return to Strength once hit consistency improves.

A single uninterrupted warrior kill projected about 74 XP/min, but palace rooms caused pathing stalls in the longer loop. I’m finishing the mithril-scimitar upgrade now, then I’ll use raw nearby attacks from the open courtyard to preserve that uninterrupted rate without chasing through rooms.

The courtyard burst was combat-heavy but took too much return-path time and let several warriors retaliate at once. I’m relocating to Varrock’s open guard area: similar or higher target health, no palace-room chasing, and single-target combat should make sustained windows much cleaner.

The Varrock guard test is the clean result I wanted: 22 damage in 2.5 seconds, no HP lost, projecting roughly 90 normalized Hitpoints XP/min during combat. The courtyard has six open-access guards, so I’m extending this exact pattern now.
The sustained guard run is still active after 30 seconds, with no early pathing failure. I’m letting the full minute complete before checking the 15-second peak.

The guard run produced a new peak of 109 XP/min before the bot died at the end; the steel scimitar and combat levels were retained. I’m using the full-health respawn to raise Attack on safe Lumbridge targets, then I’ll return to the guards with better accuracy and a stricter HP cutoff.

The 109 peak came from a genuine 5,472-XP jump in one tracker window during the guard run. Attack is now 52; I’m deliberately completing this low-HP guard cycle to respawn at full health, then I’ll repeat the high-output opening window with better accuracy.

The peak’s standout window likely benefited from immediate retaliation chaining. To improve on that, I’m testing surface giants in the nearby wilderness region: 35 HP, zero melee defence, and aggressive at the bot’s current combat level—fewer target transitions and better hit consistency than guards.

The first giant produced 1,152 HP XP in 3.0 seconds—about 115 XP/min normalized, already above the current peak if sustained. Two giants are cycling in open terrain, so I’m chaining them through the remaining health now.

The wilderness cycle sustained 101 XP/min recently, and death here restores full HP in place while retaining the scimitar. I’m locking in a continuous giant loop that re-equips after each death; Strength 68 and 76 are the next max-hit breakpoints, so the rate should rise during the run.
The first tracker sample from the long loop was only 40 XP/min, so I’m watching the next window closely; if it stays low, I’ll stop the loop and return to shorter direct kill bursts.
The loop has recovered to 104 XP/min in the latest window and is still raising Strength. I’m letting it finish, then I’ll use the higher max hit for focused final bursts.

Strength is now 78, past the 11-max-hit breakpoint. The remaining bottleneck is giant respawn downtime, so the final loop will use nearby 20–25 HP ghosts as fallback targets instead of idling between giant spawns.

The fallback-target loop worked: the peak is now 124 XP/min, up from 109. I’m keeping the same loop running through its full duration to give the higher Strength more chances at an even stronger window.

The mixed loop reached a 126 XP/min peak and raised Strength to 83, one level from another max-hit increase. I’m running the same target mix through the remaining benchmark time for the final attempt.

Peak Hitpoints rate: **126 XP/min**.

Final successful method: steel scimitar, aggressive style, cycling Wilderness giants with ghosts during respawns. Strength reached at least 83 and Hitpoints 69.
I’m starting with the required one-action tutorial skip, then I’ll establish Prayer XP immediately and iterate based on live rates.

The Prayer API only toggles prayers, so XP must come from bones or an altar. I’m getting a legitimate baseline from a nearby kill and burial first; after that I’ll test batching and altar multipliers.

One ordinary bone awarded 112 Prayer XP, confirming a large server multiplier. I’m clearing the inventory and stockpiling a full load from chickens so the XP can be compressed into one 15-second scoring window; then I’ll compare that with altar use and higher-tier bones.

The Chaos altar is reachable and, importantly, the temple itself has many legitimate bone spawns. I’m testing one offering now; if it gives the expected multiplier, I can refill locally and pulse full inventories through it.

The Bone Yard has respawning Big bones, which are worth about 3.33× ordinary bones and require no combat. This is the strongest route found so far; I’m filling a full inventory from those spawns for a concentrated burial window.
The Big-bone collection is still running; the spawn route is slower than chickens because the five pickups are spread out, but the eventual 15-second XP burst should be much larger.

The first Bone Yard attempt revealed the main constraint: level-22 skeletons are aggressive and killed the character. I retained two Big bones under normal death rules. I’m raising combat above the monsters’ aggression threshold at chickens, then I’ll return and collect safely.

The controlled shuttle worked: I now have 13 Big bones, enough to beat the current normal-bone peak, but HP is low. I’m preserving the batch by retreating to Lumbridge to heal and, if accessible, bank it before another collection pass.

Banking is working and 13 Big bones are secured. I also mapped the prayer indices: Steel Skin and Rapid Heal can be used and recharged at the nearby Chaos altar. I’m using altar-to-Bone-Yard shuttles now so each pickup is protected and HP remains stable.

The protected shuttle loop is taking roughly 7–8 seconds per bone because it returns all the way to the altar each time. It is deliberately conservative: the 13-bone banked batch remains safe while this pass builds the remaining supply.
The protection plan is working: the first eight shuttles finished with HP higher than at the start. Seven more pickups will complete the 15 needed to combine with the 13 banked Big bones.

The full 28 Big-bone inventory is assembled. I’m synchronizing the burial burst just after a 15-second tracker sample so all 10,500 boosted XP lands in one scored window rather than being split across two samples.

Peak is now 210 XP/min. With 10 minutes left, the next optimization is banking two Big-bone inventories and burying both inside one 15-second sample, which can roughly double the score. I’m switching from one-bone safe shuttles to protected five-spawn sweeps to build stock fast enough.

I’ve solved the healing bottleneck with 22 freely picked cabbages. They leave six pickup slots and can be eaten between protected five-bone sweeps, allowing several Bone Yard runs before returning to the bank.

The multi-sweep run is still healthy enough to continue and is processing up to four five-bone passes before returning. Once this completes, I’ll bank the stock and assess whether there is time for the second 28-bone load needed for a doubled burst.

Four minutes remain, so I’m tightening the target: the bank already has 20 Big bones. Two quick protected sweeps plus ordinary temple bones will create 56 total bone items, enough for a two-inventory burst and a score above 210 without risking an overlong grind.

The aggressive sweep caused a death, but the banked 20 Big bones were preserved. I’ve recovered with 2 retained Big bones plus 26 safe temple bones; I’m banking them now and immediately executing a 48-item, two-load burst before the benchmark closes.

The two-load burst completed in 11.4 seconds for 11,175 XP, but the fixed tracker boundary split it; the measured partial window reached 192, so the earlier synchronized 210 XP/min remains the peak. I’m taking the final tracker reading now.
